title: Installing a Frost-Proof Outdoor Hydrant to Deliver Hot and Cold Water Outside (This Old House)

summary: This Old House demonstrates converting a cold outdoor garden faucet into a year-round, hot-and-cold wall hydrant that feeds exterior water with a frost-proof design. The host explains the drawbacks of a simple Y-connector approach, then installs a frost-proof wall hydrant that mounts on the exterior, with hot and cold runs brought from inside. The process covers routing copper supply from a kitchen-area crawl space, turning off the main, cutting the copper line, removing the old faucet, positioning the new hydrant (center-to-center = 5 inches), sealing the unit to vinyl with silicone, securing it with weather screws, and tying hot and cold lines together with shut-offs for future service. The final section demonstrates turning the water back on and testing the new outside faucet, which now provides hot water outdoors and eliminates winter shutoffs inside. The lesson emphasizes freeze protection and the convenience of year-round use for outdoor tasks like washing the car or pets.
topics: Cutting copper with a pipe cutter (compact cutter)

sections.title: Initial concept: add hot water to the outdoor faucet
sections.description: The host compares a DIY hot-water add-on to a dedicated frost-proof hydrant, explaining that a simple Y-connector approach can be bulky and clunky, and introduces the frost-proof wall hydrant as a cleaner alternative.

sections.title: What a frost-proof wall hydrant is and why it’s better
sections.description: Explanation of how hot and cold meet at the faucet body, with the important note that the frost-proof design keeps the water shut off inside the conditioned space to prevent freezing and to avoid water presence outside the wall.

sections.title: Site assessment and routing plan
sections.description: The crew identifies the crawl space as the work area, traces the water main rising through the floor, notes a kitchen-area water meter, and identifies the hot and cold lines feeding the exterior faucet.

sections.title: Workspace prep and initial rough-in
sections.description: To create room for work, the disposer is removed and the main water supply is shut off to begin cutting and reconfiguring the lines for the new hydrant.

sections.title: Cutting and removing the old faucet
sections.description: Using a compact cutter, the copper line is cut and the existing garden faucet is removed to prepare for the new vertical wall hydrant installation.

sections.title: Positioning and spacing for the new hydrant
sections.description: The new faucet's center-to-center distance is set at five inches, ensuring proper alignment with the new wall hydrant mounting and existing piping.

sections.title: Prepare hydrant and seal
sections.description: The stem is loosened and removed to protect the washer while soldering extension pieces. A thick bead of silicone is applied to the hydrant’s back to seal against vinyl mounting.

sections.title: Mounting and securing the hydrant
sections.description: The hydrant is secured to the wall with weather-resistant screws, ensuring a watertight attachment and proper exterior mounting.

sections.title: Connect hot and cold lines and add shut-offs
sections.description: Inside-out plumbing work continues: copper piping is run to the hydrant, shut-off valves are added for future service, and the hot and cold lines are arranged to meet at the wall hydrant.

sections.title: Test and final result
sections.description: Water is turned back on and the new wall hydrant provides both hot and cold water outdoors. The host notes the advantage of year-round usability without interior shut-offs, and the test confirms proper operation.
